Chapter 17 — Circles

Kanna, keep finding the centre and drawing a radius. Most circle formulas come from one right triangle.

Your overall target remains 200 marks: Physics 60, Maths 60, Chemistry 80. First secure the centre, radius, diameter, chord and line-intersection ideas. Then connect tangency, two-circle geometry and the supporting source tools.

Important for JEE Main: the official unit explicitly names the standard/general circle equation, centre and radius, a circle from diameter endpoints, and intersections of a line with an origin-centred circle. Learn those core ideas first. Tangent/chord geometry supports many supplied questions. Pole–polar, radical centre, orthogonal circles and the director-circle name are supporting extensions in this PDF; we explain the needed results without treating each as a separately named official syllabus requirement.

Concept C01 — A circle is a fixed distance from one fixed point

The fixed point is the centre, C=(h,k)C=(h,k)C=(h,k). The fixed positive distance is the radius, rrr. Every point P=(x,y)P=(x,y)P=(x,y) on the circle satisfies CP=rCP=rCP=r.

Using the distance formula and squaring,

(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2,r>0.\boxed{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2},\qquad r>0.(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2​,r>0.

The disc includes the interior: (x−h)2+(y−k)2≤r2(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2\le r^2(x−h)2+(y−k)2≤r2. The circle itself is only the boundary.

Expand and compare:

x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0⟺(x+g)2+(y+f)2=g2+f2−c.x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x+g)^2+(y+f)^2=g^2+f^2-c.x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0⟺(x+g)2+(y+f)2=g2+f2−c.

Thus

C=(−g,−f),r2=g2+f2−c.\boxed{C=(-g,-f),\qquad r^2=g^2+f^2-c}.C=(−g,−f),r2=g2+f2−c​.

Why the centre signs reverse: the horizontal square is (x−h)2=x2−2hx+h2(x-h)^2=x^2-2hx+h^2(x−h)2=x2−2hx+h2, so the xxx coefficient is −2h-2h−2h.

Three cases matter:

  • r2>0r^2>0r2>0: a real circle with positive radius.
  • r2=0r^2=0r2=0: just the one point (−g,−f)(-g,-f)(−g,−f), called a point circle.
  • r2<0r^2<0r2<0: no real points, because two real squares cannot add to a negative number.

If the coefficients of x2,y2x^2,y^2x2,y2 are the same nonzero number AAA, divide the whole equation by AAA first. A general quadratic with an xyxyxy term or unequal squared coefficients is not automatically a circle in these rectangular coordinates.

Useful geometry:

diameter=2r,circumference=2πr,disc area=πr2.\text{diameter}=2r,\qquad \text{circumference}=2\pi r,\qquad \text{disc area}=\pi r^2.diameter=2r,circumference=2πr,disc area=πr2.

A point on the circle can be written (h+rcos⁡θ,k+rsin⁡θ)(h+r\cos\theta,k+r\sin\theta)(h+rcosθ,k+rsinθ). Here θ\thetaθ is the direction of its radius; this parametrization is useful for plotting and angle questions.

Concept C02 — Build a circle from the information given

Centre and one boundary point: substitute the point into (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2 to find r2r^2r2.

Diameter endpoints A(x1,y1),B(x2,y2)A(x_1,y_1),B(x_2,y_2)A(x1​,y1​),B(x2​,y2​): the centre is their midpoint and the radius is AB/2AB/2AB/2. Equivalently,

(x−x1)(x−x2)+(y−y1)(y−y2)=0.\boxed{(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0}.(x−x1​)(x−x2​)+(y−y1​)(y−y2​)=0​.

Why does the product formula work? The angle APBAPBAPB is 90∘90^\circ90∘ for a point PPP on the circle with diameter ABABAB. So (P−A)⋅(P−B)=0(P-A)\cdot(P-B)=0(P−A)⋅(P−B)=0, which expands into the displayed equation.

Three noncollinear points: substitute them into x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0 and solve the three linear equations for g,f,cg,f,cg,f,c. Such points determine one circle. Three distinct collinear points cannot lie on one nondegenerate circle.

Centre on a given line: combine that line with equal distances to known boundary points. Subtracting the two squared-distance equations cancels h2+k2h^2+k^2h2+k2 and produces another line, the perpendicular bisector.

Passing through the origin: substitution gives c=0c=0c=0. If its other positive axis intercepts are a,ba,ba,b, the circle is

x2+y2−ax−by=0,C=(a/2,b/2),r=a2+b22.x^2+y^2-ax-by=0,\qquad C=(a/2,b/2),\quad r=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}2.x2+y2−ax−by=0,C=(a/2,b/2),r=2a2+b2​​.

The two nonzero axis endpoints form the diameter: their joining segment is opposite the right angle at the origin.

Concept C03 — A point's power tells inside, on or outside

For S(x,y)=x2+y2+2gx+2fy+cS(x,y)=x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+cS(x,y)=x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c, put P=(x0,y0)P=(x_0,y_0)P=(x0​,y0​):

S(P)=CP2−r2.\boxed{S(P)=CP^2-r^2}.S(P)=CP2−r2​.

So S(P)<0S(P)<0S(P)<0 means inside, S(P)=0S(P)=0S(P)=0 means on the circle, and S(P)>0S(P)>0S(P)>0 means outside.

This number is called the power of the point. It is a squared-length difference, not the ordinary distance from the circumference.

For an external point with tangent touching at TTT, the radius CTCTCT is perpendicular to PTPTPT. Pythagoras gives

PT2=CP2−r2=S(P),PT=S(P).\boxed{PT^2=CP^2-r^2=S(P),\qquad PT=\sqrt{S(P)}}.PT2=CP2−r2=S(P),PT=S(P)​​.

If a secant from an external point meets the circle at A,BA,BA,B, then PA⋅PB=S(P)PA\cdot PB=S(P)PA⋅PB=S(P) with both ordinary distances taken along that ray. For an inside point, the two directed intersection distances have opposite signs; their product is negative, matching S(P)S(P)S(P). Do not take a square root of a negative power and call it a real tangent length: no real tangents start inside the circle.

Concept C04 — A line cuts, touches or misses a circle

Let ddd be the perpendicular distance from the centre to a line.

Compare Geometry Number of distinct intersections
d<rd<rd<r cuts a chord 2
d=rd=rd=r tangent, meaning one touching point 1
d>rd>rd>r misses the circle 0

For ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0ax+by+c=0,

d=∣ah+bk+c∣a2+b2.d=\frac{|ah+bk+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}.d=a2+b2​∣ah+bk+c∣​.

Important for JEE Main: this test works for sloping, vertical and horizontal lines.

If the line cuts a chord ABABAB, its perpendicular foot HHH from the centre is the chord's midpoint. The two right triangles CHA,CHBCHA,CHBCHA,CHB have the same hypotenuse rrr and common leg CHCHCH, so their remaining legs are equal:

AH=BH=r2−d2,AB=2r2−d2.AH=BH=\sqrt{r^2-d^2}, \qquad \boxed{AB=2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}}.AH=BH=r2−d2​,AB=2r2−d2​​.

To find intersection coordinates: substitute the line into the circle to get a quadratic. Positive, zero and negative discriminants give two, one and no real intersection points. Handle a vertical line by substituting its fixed xxx directly.

Efficient coordinate construction: if HHH is the foot and u\mathbf uu is a unit vector along the line, then

A,B=H±r2−d2 u.A,B=H\pm\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\,\mathbf u.A,B=H±r2−d2​u.

This finds both endpoints without expanding a quadratic. A chord cannot be longer than the diameter 2r2r2r.

Concept C05 — A tangent at a boundary point is normal to the radius

At a point PPP on a circle, the tangent is perpendicular to CPCPCP. For an origin-centred circle and P=(x1,y1)P=(x_1,y_1)P=(x1​,y1​),

(x1,y1)⋅(x−x1,y−y1)=0.(x_1,y_1)\cdot(x-x_1,y-y_1)=0.(x1​,y1​)⋅(x−x1​,y−y1​)=0.

Since x12+y12=r2x_1^2+y_1^2=r^2x12​+y12​=r2, this becomes

xx1+yy1=r2.\boxed{xx_1+yy_1=r^2}.xx1​+yy1​=r2​.

For centre C=(h,k)C=(h,k)C=(h,k), use the shifted version

(x1−h)(x−h)+(y1−k)(y−k)=r2.\boxed{(x_1-h)(x-h)+(y_1-k)(y-k)=r^2}.(x1​−h)(x−h)+(y1​−k)(y−k)=r2​.

For the general equation S=0S=0S=0, the same tangent can be written

T=xx1+yy1+g(x+x1)+f(y+y1)+c=0.\boxed{T=xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)+c=0}.T=xx1​+yy1​+g(x+x1​)+f(y+y1​)+c=0​.

Condition: PPP must lie on the circle for this to be its tangent at PPP. If PPP is external, the same expression has a different meaning, taught in C12.

For an unknown finite slope mmm, write y=mx+by=mx+by=mx+b and impose the centre-to-line distance rrr. This gives

b=k−mh±r1+m2.\boxed{b=k-mh\pm r\sqrt{1+m^2}}.b=k−mh±r1+m2​​.

The extra vertical tangents are x=h±rx=h\pm rx=h±r. Slope form does not include them.

Concept C06 — Two tangents from an external point

Tangents from the same external point PPP have equal lengths: both equal CP2−r2\sqrt{CP^2-r^2}CP2−r2​. The right triangles CAP,CBPCAP,CBPCAP,CBP have common hypotenuse CPCPCP and equal radii CA,CBCA,CBCA,CB, so they are congruent. Thus CPCPCP also bisects the angle at PPP.

If θ=∠APB\theta=\angle APBθ=∠APB is the angle between the two tangent segments from PPP,

sin⁡(θ/2)=rCP,CP>r.\boxed{\sin(\theta/2)=\frac r{CP}},\qquad CP>r.sin(θ/2)=CPr​​,CP>r.

Infinite supporting lines also make the supplementary angle 180∘−θ180^\circ-\theta180∘−θ. State which angle the question means; the picture with rays from PPP removes the ambiguity.

The quadrilateral CAPBCAPBCAPB is two right triangles:

area=rCP2−r2.\boxed{\text{area}=r\sqrt{CP^2-r^2}}.area=rCP2−r2​​.

If ϕ=∠ACB\phi=\angle ACBϕ=∠ACB is the smaller central angle between the contact radii, then ϕ+θ=180∘\phi+\theta=180^\circϕ+θ=180∘ for this quadrilateral.

Perpendicular tangents: when θ=90∘\theta=90^\circθ=90∘, CP2=2r2CP^2=2r^2CP2=2r2. Their starting points form the director circle:

(x−h)2+(y−k)2=2r2.\boxed{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=2r^2}.(x−h)2+(y−k)2=2r2​.

The name is a supporting source term. Its meaning is just the locus of points from which the tangent segments meet at 90∘90^\circ90∘. The two right triangles are then isosceles, and the quadrilateral is a square.

Concept C07 — Two-circle position decides the tangent count

Let the two positive radii be r1,r2r_1,r_2r1​,r2​, and let the centre distance be ddd. Compare ddd with their sum and absolute difference.

Position Condition Common tangent lines
separate, outside each other d>r1+r2d>r_1+r_2d>r1​+r2​ 4
touch externally d=r1+r2d=r_1+r_2d=r1​+r2​ 3
cross at two points ∣r1−r2∣<d<r1+r2|r_1-r_2|<d<r_1+r_2∣r1​−r2​∣<d<r1​+r2​ 2
touch internally d=∣r1−r2∣>0d=|r_1-r_2|>0d=∣r1​−r2​∣>0 1

A common tangent touches both circles. At external contact, the two internal tangents merge into the one tangent at the touching point; this is why the count becomes 3. At internal contact, only the touching-point tangent remains.

Pattern: for external touching of a variable circle with radius ρ\rhoρ, write centre distance r+ρr+\rhor+ρ. For internal touching, use ∣r−ρ∣|r-\rho|∣r−ρ∣ and check which circle contains which.

Concept C08 — Common tangent length comes from one right triangle

Here “length” means the distance between the two touching points, not the length of an infinite line.

For a direct common tangent, the centres are on the same side of the line. Their perpendicular radius offsets differ by r1−r2r_1-r_2r1​−r2​:

Ldirect=d2−(r1−r2)2.\boxed{L_{\rm direct}=\sqrt{d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2}}.Ldirect​=d2−(r1​−r2​)2​​.

For a transverse/internal common tangent, the centres are on opposite sides. The perpendicular offsets add:

Linternal=d2−(r1+r2)2.\boxed{L_{\rm internal}=\sqrt{d^2-(r_1+r_2)^2}}.Linternal​=d2−(r1​+r2​)2​​.

Use these only when the relevant tangent exists. A positive internal segment needs d>r1+r2d>r_1+r_2d>r1​+r2​; at external contact its limiting length is zero. The centre-to-centre distance ddd is the hypotenuse, not the tangent segment.

Concept C09 — Common chord, radical axis and a circle family

At a shared point of two circles S1=0,S2=0S_1=0,S_2=0S1​=0,S2​=0, both equations hold. Subtracting cancels x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2:

S1−S2=0.\boxed{S_1-S_2=0}.S1​−S2​=0​.

If they intersect at two points, this is the common chord's line. Its direction is perpendicular to the line joining the centres.

More generally, S1=S2S_1=S_2S1​=S2​ means a point has the same power to both circles. This line is the radical axis, even when the circles do not meet. It need not contain real circle-intersection points. Concentric distinct circles have no finite radical-axis line.

For three circles, intersect two independent radical axes to find the radical centre. Test the third power as a check. Some configurations have parallel or coincident axes, so a unique finite radical centre is not guaranteed in every imaginable case.

Circle through common points of a circle S=0S=0S=0 and line L=0L=0L=0:

S+λL=0.\boxed{S+\lambda L=0}.S+λL=0​.

At a shared point both terms vanish for every λ\lambdaλ. A further point fixes λ\lambdaλ. This is useful when computing the common points would create unnecessary radicals.

For two circles normalized to the same squared coefficients, a full family through their common points can be written λS1+μS2=0\lambda S_1+\mu S_2=0λS1​+μS2​=0. To obtain a proper circle, require λ+μ≠0\lambda+\mu\ne0λ+μ=0; when the squared coefficients cancel, the member is their radical-axis line instead.

Concept C10 — Orthogonal circles: perpendicular tangents at a crossing

“Orthogonal” means the two circles cross with tangents at 90∘90^\circ90∘. Rotating both tangent directions by 90∘90^\circ90∘ gives their radii, so those radii are perpendicular too.

At a crossing PPP, triangle C1PC2C_1PC_2C1​PC2​ is right-angled at PPP:

C1C22=r12+r22.\boxed{C_1C_2^2=r_1^2+r_2^2}.C1​C22​=r12​+r22​​.

For Si=x2+y2+2gix+2fiy+ci=0S_i=x^2+y^2+2g_ix+2f_iy+c_i=0Si​=x2+y2+2gi​x+2fi​y+ci​=0, expanding the same condition gives

2g1g2+2f1f2=c1+c2.\boxed{2g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_2}.2g1​g2​+2f1​f2​=c1​+c2​​.

This is a supporting shortcut. The right-triangle meaning is safer than remembering an isolated coefficient identity. Positive radii together with d2=r12+r22d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2d2=r12​+r22​ place the centres between the internal and external touching limits, so actual crossings exist.

Concept C11 — A chord's midpoint gives its perpendicular direction

If MMM is the midpoint of a nonzero chord, the centre-to-midpoint line is perpendicular to the chord. For an origin-centred radius-rrr circle and M=(h,k)≠(0,0)M=(h,k)\ne(0,0)M=(h,k)=(0,0),

hx+ky=h2+k2.\boxed{hx+ky=h^2+k^2}.hx+ky=h2+k2​.

Why? (h,k)(h,k)(h,k) is the chord's normal, and the line passes through (h,k)(h,k)(h,k). Check that h2+k2<r2h^2+k^2<r^2h2+k2<r2 for a genuine nonzero chord.

If MMM is the centre, many diameters share that midpoint; the displayed equation reduces to 0=00=00=0 and cannot select one chord.

For a known chord endpoint AAA and midpoint MMM, the other endpoint is B=2M−AB=2M-AB=2M−A. Substitute it into the circle equation to find a midpoint locus. This route automatically keeps track of endpoints.

Locus warning: a derived equation can contain a zero-length chord's midpoint. Remove it if the original construction requires two different endpoints.

Concept C12 — Chord of contact, polar and pole

These names are supporting source tools. Begin with the actual geometry.

From an external point P=(x1,y1)P=(x_1,y_1)P=(x1​,y1​), draw two tangents touching the circle at A,BA,BA,B. The segment ABABAB is the chord of contact: it joins the two touching points, not the external point to the centre.

For x2+y2=r2x^2+y^2=r^2x2+y2=r2, the tangent at A=(a,b)A=(a,b)A=(a,b) has equation ax+by=r2ax+by=r^2ax+by=r2. Since it passes through PPP,

ax1+by1=r2.ax_1+by_1=r^2.ax1​+by1​=r2.

So AAA lies on xx1+yy1=r2xx_1+yy_1=r^2xx1​+yy1​=r2. The same argument holds for BBB, giving

chord of contact: xx1+yy1=r2.\boxed{\text{chord of contact: }xx_1+yy_1=r^2}.chord of contact: xx1​+yy1​=r2​.

The same line formula, associated with a general point PPP relative to the circle, is called its polar. The point is the pole of that line. When PPP is external, the polar is the real chord-of-contact line. When PPP is on the circle, it is its tangent. For an inside point other than the centre, the polar still exists algebraically but is not a chord joining real tangent contacts.

For an origin-centred circle and a line ax+by=dax+by=dax+by=d with d≠0d\ne0d=0,

pole=(r2ad,r2bd).\boxed{\text{pole}=\left(\frac{r^2a}{d},\frac{r^2b}{d}\right)}.pole=(dr2a​,dr2b​)​.

Compare coefficients after rewriting the line with right side r2r^2r2. A line through the centre has no finite pole in this formula; do not divide by d=0d=0d=0.

For a shifted circle, the polar of PPP is (x1−h)(x−h)+(y1−k)(y−k)=r2(x_1-h)(x-h)+(y_1-k)(y-k)=r^2(x1​−h)(x−h)+(y1​−k)(y−k)=r2. In the general S=0S=0S=0 notation, it is T=0T=0T=0 from C05. State whether it represents a tangent or a contact chord before applying the same algebraic expression.

Concept C13 — Axis intercepts and touching an axis

A circle touches the xxx-axis when the centre's vertical distance is its radius:

∣k∣=r.|k|=r.∣k∣=r.

It touches the yyy-axis when ∣h∣=r|h|=r∣h∣=r. A circle in the first quadrant touching both axes therefore has centre (r,r)(r,r)(r,r), with r>0r>0r>0.

A circle touching the xxx-axis at (a,0)(a,0)(a,0) has centre (a,k)(a,k)(a,k) and radius ∣k∣|k|∣k∣:

(x−a)2+(y−k)2=k2.(x-a)^2+(y-k)^2=k^2.(x−a)2+(y−k)2=k2.

Use a supplied boundary point to find kkk; do not assume the centre is above the axis until the data determines it.

Intercept versus tangency: an intercept on an axis is the chord cut by that axis. Put the other coordinate equal to zero and find both roots.

For x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0:

x-axis chord length=2g2−c,y-axis chord length=2f2−c,\boxed{\text{$x$-axis chord length}=2\sqrt{g^2-c}},\qquad \boxed{\text{$y$-axis chord length}=2\sqrt{f^2-c}},x-axis chord length=2g2−c​​,y-axis chord length=2f2−c​​,

when the square-root inputs are positive. Zero means tangency; negative means no real intercept. These are chord lengths, not the coordinates of their endpoints.

Concept C14 — Nearest and farthest points on a circle

Let d=CPd=CPd=CP for a fixed point PPP. For a point QQQ on the circumference,

PQmax⁡=d+r,PQmin⁡=∣d−r∣.\boxed{PQ_{\max}=d+r,\qquad PQ_{\min}=|d-r|}.PQmax​=d+r,PQmin​=∣d−r∣​.

Both extremes lie on the line through C,PC,PC,P. If P=CP=CP=C, every circumference point has distance rrr.

For d>0d>0d>0, the nearest point is C+rd(P−C)C+\frac r d(P-C)C+dr​(P−C), and the farthest is C−rd(P−C)C-\frac r d(P-C)C−dr​(P−C). The triangle inequality proves the upper bound PQ≤PC+CQ=d+rPQ\le PC+CQ=d+rPQ≤PC+CQ=d+r; the reverse triangle inequality proves the lower bound.

If the allowed set is the filled disc, the shortest distance is max⁡(0,d−r)\max(0,d-r)max(0,d−r), because an inside point itself is allowed. Read whether the question says circumference or disc.

Another useful bound — Cauchy–Schwarz, important for JEE Main: for real coordinates,

(au+bv)2≤(a2+b2)(u2+v2).(au+bv)^2\le(a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2).(au+bv)2≤(a2+b2)(u2+v2).

The difference is (av−bu)2≥0(av-bu)^2\ge0(av−bu)2≥0, so the result follows from a square being nonnegative. Equality means the two coordinate pairs are parallel, including the appropriate zero cases. On u2+v2=r2u^2+v^2=r^2u2+v2=r2, it bounds a dot product by ra2+b2r\sqrt{a^2+b^2}ra2+b2​. This is useful when a squared-distance expansion contains a linear expression such as 3x+4y3x+4y3x+4y. Q28 shows the full connection to the opposite radius direction.

Worked solutions to the 35 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Complete the squares to see the centre

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C01

The centre and radius of the circle x2+y2−6x+8y−11=0x^2+y^2-6x+8y-11=0x2+y2−6x+8y−11=0 are

  • (a) (−3,4)(-3,4)(−3,4) and 666
  • (b) (3,−4)(3,-4)(3,−4) and 666
  • (c) (3,−4)(3,-4)(3,−4) and 363636
  • (d) (3,−4)(3,-4)(3,−4) and 14\sqrt{14}14​

The centre is easiest to see after completing squares. Group the xxx and yyy terms:

x2−6x+y2+8y=11.x^2-6x+y^2+8y=11.x2−6x+y2+8y=11.

Add 9 and 16 to complete both squares:

(x−3)2+(y+4)2=11+9+16=36.(x-3)^2+(y+4)^2=11+9+16=36.(x−3)2+(y+4)2=11+9+16=36.

Compare with (x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2:

C=(3,−4),r=6;(b).\boxed{C=(3,-4),\quad r=6;\quad\text{(b)}}.C=(3,−4),r=6;(b)​.

Check: moving 6 units right from the centre gives (9,−4)(9,-4)(9,−4). Substitution into the original equation gives 81+16−54−32−11=081+16-54-32-11=081+16−54−32−11=0.

Another possible approach: g=−3,f=4,c=−11g=-3,f=4,c=-11g=−3,f=4,c=−11, so C=(−g,−f)=(3,−4)C=(-g,-f)=(3,-4)C=(−g,−f)=(3,−4) and r=9+16+11=6r=\sqrt{9+16+11}=6r=9+16+11​=6. Completing squares explains the signs; coefficient reading is faster once that meaning is secure. The number 36 is r2r^2r2, not rrr.

Question 2 — The three axis points form a right triangle

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C02

A circle passes through the origin and cuts off intercepts 444 and 666 on the xxx-axis and yyy-axis respectively (both positive). Its radius is

  • (a) 52\sqrt{52}52​
  • (b) 555
  • (c) 101010
  • (d) 13\sqrt{13}13​

Which three points are on the circle? They are O=(0,0)O=(0,0)O=(0,0), A=(4,0)A=(4,0)A=(4,0), B=(0,6)B=(0,6)B=(0,6). The two axis segments OA,OBOA,OBOA,OB are perpendicular.

The side opposite a right angle in an inscribed triangle is a diameter. Thus

AB=42+62=52=213,r=AB/2=13;(d).AB=\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}, \qquad \boxed{r=AB/2=\sqrt{13};\quad\text{(d)}}.AB=42+62​=52​=213​,r=AB/2=13​;(d)​.

Another possible approach: because the circle passes through the origin, write x2+y2+2gx+2fy=0x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy=0x2+y2+2gx+2fy=0. The other points give

16+8g=0⇒g=−2,36+12f=0⇒f=−3.16+8g=0\Rightarrow g=-2,\qquad 36+12f=0\Rightarrow f=-3.16+8g=0⇒g=−2,36+12f=0⇒f=−3.

So the centre is (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) and r2=4+9=13r^2=4+9=13r2=4+9=13. Its squared distance from each of O,A,BO,A,BO,A,B is 13, checking both the geometry and algebra.

Question 3 — A tangent makes a right triangle with the radius

PDF page 86 | Numerical value | Notes: C03,C06

The length of the tangent drawn from the point (6,5)(6,5)(6,5) to the circle x2+y2−2x−4y−4=0x^2+y^2-2x-4y-4=0x2+y2−2x−4y−4=0 is ____.

A tangent length is one leg of a right triangle. Complete squares to find the centre and radius:

(x−1)2+(y−2)2=9.(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=9.(x−1)2+(y−2)2=9.

For P=(6,5)P=(6,5)P=(6,5), CP2=(6−1)2+(5−2)2=34CP^2=(6-1)^2+(5-2)^2=34CP2=(6−1)2+(5−2)2=34. Since 34>934>934>9, PPP is external and real tangents exist.

At a contact TTT, CT⊥PTCT\perp PTCT⊥PT, so

PT2=CP2−CT2=34−9=25⟹PT=5.PT^2=CP^2-CT^2=34-9=25 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{PT=5}.PT2=CP2−CT2=34−9=25⟹PT=5​.

Another possible approach — point power: substitute PPP into the normalized circle expression:

S(P)=36+25−12−20−4=25.S(P)=36+25-12-20-4=25.S(P)=36+25−12−20−4=25.

The tangent length is S(P)=5\sqrt{S(P)}=5S(P)​=5. The radius-right-triangle derivation explains why substituting into a circle equation gives a squared tangent length here.

Question 4 — Tangency means centre-to-line distance equals radius

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C04

If the line 3x+4y=k3x+4y=k3x+4y=k (k>0k>0k>0) touches the circle x2+y2=4x^2+y^2=4x2+y2=4, then k=k=k=

  • (a) 555
  • (b) 222
  • (c) 101010
  • (d) 202020

“Touches” means the line is exactly one radius from the centre. The centre is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and radius 2.

For 3x+4y−k=03x+4y-k=03x+4y−k=0, the centre distance is

d=∣−k∣32+42=∣k∣5.d=\frac{|-k|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=\frac{|k|}{5}.d=32+42​∣−k∣​=5∣k∣​.

Tangency requires ∣k∣/5=2|k|/5=2∣k∣/5=2, so k=±10k=\pm10k=±10. The question gives k>0k>0k>0:

k=10;(c).\boxed{k=10;\quad\text{(c)}}.k=10;(c)​.

Check: its foot from the origin is (6/5,8/5)(6/5,8/5)(6/5,8/5), which has squared distance (36+64)/25=4(36+64)/25=4(36+64)/25=4 and satisfies 3x+4y=103x+4y=103x+4y=10.

Another possible approach: substitute y=(k−3x)/4y=(k-3x)/4y=(k−3x)/4 into x2+y2=4x^2+y^2=4x2+y2=4 and demand a repeated real root. This gives the same k2=100k^2=100k2=100, but uses more expansion than the centre-distance test.

Question 5 — The tangent is perpendicular to the actual radius

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The equation of the tangent to the circle x2+y2=25x^2+y^2=25x2+y2=25 at the point (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) is

  • (a) 4x+3y=254x+3y=254x+3y=25
  • (b) 3x−4y=253x-4y=253x−4y=25
  • (c) 3x+4y=253x+4y=253x+4y=25
  • (d) 3x+4y=53x+4y=53x+4y=5

Draw the radius to the given point. P=(3,4)P=(3,4)P=(3,4) lies on the circle because 32+42=253^2+4^2=2532+42=25. The radius direction is (3,4)(3,4)(3,4), so this is the tangent's normal.

The line through PPP with that normal is

3(x−3)+4(y−4)=0⟹3x+4y=25;(c).3(x-3)+4(y-4)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{3x+4y=25;\quad\text{(c)}}.3(x−3)+4(y−4)=0⟹3x+4y=25;(c)​.

Check: the line passes through (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) and its distance from the origin is 25/5=525/5=525/5=5, the circle radius.

Another possible approach: differentiate x2+y2=25x^2+y^2=25x2+y2=25:

2x+2yy′=0,y′(3,4)=−34.2x+2yy'=0,\qquad y'(3,4)=-\frac34.2x+2yy′=0,y′(3,4)=−43​.

Then y−4=−(3/4)(x−3)y-4=-(3/4)(x-3)y−4=−(3/4)(x−3) gives the same line. The normal-vector route also works at vertical tangents, where dividing by y=0y=0y=0 would fail.

Question 6 — The perpendicular from the centre halves a chord

PDF page 86 | Numerical value | Notes: C04

The line 3x+4y=103x+4y=103x+4y=10 cuts the circle x2+y2=13x^2+y^2=13x2+y2=13 in a chord. The length of the chord is ____.

The chord splits into two equal pieces at the perpendicular foot. Let HHH be the foot from the origin to 3x+4y=103x+4y=103x+4y=10.

CH=105=2,r2=13.CH=\frac{10}{5}=2,\qquad r^2=13.CH=510​=2,r2=13.

For a chord endpoint AAA, triangle CHACHACHA is right:

AH2=CA2−CH2=13−4=9.AH^2=CA^2-CH^2=13-4=9.AH2=CA2−CH2=13−4=9.

So AH=3AH=3AH=3, and the full chord is

AB=2AH=6.\boxed{AB=2AH=6}.AB=2AH=6​.

Another possible approach — actual endpoints: the foot is H=(6/5,8/5)H=(6/5,8/5)H=(6/5,8/5) and a unit direction along the chord is (4/5,−3/5)(4/5,-3/5)(4/5,−3/5). Hence

A,B=H±3(4/5,−3/5)=(185,−15), (−65,175).A,B=H\pm3(4/5,-3/5) =\left(\frac{18}5,-\frac15\right),\ \left(-\frac65,\frac{17}5\right).A,B=H±3(4/5,−3/5)=(518​,−51​), (−56​,517​).

Each point satisfies the line and has x2+y2=13x^2+y^2=13x2+y2=13. Their distance is 6. This is a useful independent check when coordinates are also needed.

Question 7 — Subtract circle equations to find their shared chord line

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C09

The length of the common chord of the circles x2+y2=16x^2+y^2=16x2+y2=16 and x2+y2−8x=0x^2+y^2-8x=0x2+y2−8x=0 is

  • (a) 232\sqrt323​
  • (b) 888
  • (c) 666
  • (d) 434\sqrt343​

A shared point satisfies both circle equations. Subtract them before finding coordinates:

(x2+y2)−(x2+y2−8x)=16−0⟹x=2.(x^2+y^2)-(x^2+y^2-8x)=16-0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=2.(x2+y2)−(x2+y2−8x)=16−0⟹x=2.

On the first circle,

4+y2=16⟹y=±23.4+y^2=16\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\pm2\sqrt3.4+y2=16⟹y=±23​.

The chord is vertical, so subtract its endpoint heights:

AB=23−(−23)=43;(d).\boxed{AB=2\sqrt3-(-2\sqrt3)=4\sqrt3;\quad\text{(d)}}.AB=23​−(−23​)=43​;(d)​.

Another possible approach: both circles have radius 4, with centres (0,0),(4,0)(0,0),(4,0)(0,0),(4,0). Their shared chord is halfway between the equal centres, so it is 2 units from either. The chord formula gives 216−4=432\sqrt{16-4}=4\sqrt3216−4​=43​.

Check: the result is positive and below the diameter 8. Subtracting the circle equations found a line, not the chord length itself.

Question 8 — First decide how the two circles meet

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C07

The number of common tangents to the circles x2+y2=4x^2+y^2=4x2+y2=4 and x2+y2−6x−8y+16=0x^2+y^2-6x-8y+16=0x2+y2−6x−8y+16=0 is

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 333
  • (c) 222
  • (d) 444

Count tangents only after classifying the circles. The first has centre (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), radius 2. For the second,

(x−3)2+(y−4)2=9,(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=9,(x−3)2+(y−4)2=9,

so its centre is (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) and radius 3. The centre distance is d=9+16=5d=\sqrt{9+16}=5d=9+16​=5.

Since d=r1+r2=2+3d=r_1+r_2=2+3d=r1​+r2​=2+3, they touch externally. There are two common tangents around their outer sides and one at the contact point:

3 common tangents;(b).\boxed{3\ \text{common tangents};\quad\text{(b)}}.3 common tangents;(b)​.

Why not four? For two separate circles, two transverse tangents cross the gap. As the circles approach external contact, those two merge into one touching-point tangent. The outer two remain.

Check: the touching point is (6/5,8/5)(6/5,8/5)(6/5,8/5) along the centre segment. Its line 3x+4y=103x+4y=103x+4y=10 is distance 2 from the first centre and 3 from the second, confirming the extra shared tangent.

Question 9 — Orthogonal circles have perpendicular radii at their crossing

PDF page 86 | Numerical value | Notes: C10

If the circles x2+y2+2x+4y−3=0x^2+y^2+2x+4y-3=0x2+y2+2x+4y−3=0 and x2+y2−4x−2y+k=0x^2+y^2-4x-2y+k=0x2+y2−4x−2y+k=0 are orthogonal, then k=k=k= ____.

Orthogonal means perpendicular tangents at a crossing. The radii to that point are perpendicular as well, making a right triangle between the two centres.

For the first circle,

C1=(−1,−2),r12=1+4+3=8.C_1=(-1,-2),\qquad r_1^2=1+4+3=8.C1​=(−1,−2),r12​=1+4+3=8.

For the second,

C2=(2,1),r22=4+1−k=5−k.C_2=(2,1),\qquad r_2^2=4+1-k=5-k.C2​=(2,1),r22​=4+1−k=5−k.

Thus

C1C22=32+32=18=r12+r22=8+5−k,C_1C_2^2=3^2+3^2=18=r_1^2+r_2^2=8+5-k,C1​C22​=32+32=18=r12​+r22​=8+5−k,

giving

k=−5.\boxed{k=-5}.k=−5​.

Check: r22=10>0r_2^2=10>0r22​=10>0, and 18\sqrt{18}18​ lies strictly between ∣10−8∣|\sqrt{10}-\sqrt8|∣10​−8​∣ and 10+8\sqrt{10}+\sqrt810​+8​, so actual crossings exist.

Another possible approach: use 2g1g2+2f1f2=c1+c22g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_22g1​g2​+2f1​f2​=c1​+c2​. It gives 2(1)(−2)+2(2)(−1)=−3+k2(1)(-2)+2(2)(-1)=-3+k2(1)(−2)+2(2)(−1)=−3+k, hence −8=−3+k-8=-3+k−8=−3+k and k=−5k=-5k=−5. The geometric version makes the sign and meaning easier to remember.

Question 10 — Midpoints of chords through one boundary point have a smaller-circle locus

PDF page 86 | MCQ | Notes: C11

The locus of the midpoints of the chords of the circle x2+y2−4x=0x^2+y^2-4x=0x2+y2−4x=0 that pass through the origin is

  • (a) x2+y2−4x=0x^2+y^2-4x=0x2+y2−4x=0
  • (b) x2+y2−x=0x^2+y^2-x=0x2+y2−x=0
  • (c) x2+y2−2x−4=0x^2+y^2-2x-4=0x2+y2−2x−4=0
  • (d) x2+y2−2x=0x^2+y^2-2x=0x2+y2−2x=0

Use the endpoint–midpoint relation first. One endpoint is O=(0,0)O=(0,0)O=(0,0). If the midpoint is M=(x,y)M=(x,y)M=(x,y), the other endpoint must be B=(2x,2y)B=(2x,2y)B=(2x,2y).

Since BBB lies on the original circle,

(2x)2+(2y)2−4(2x)=0⟹x2+y2−2x=0;intended (d).(2x)^2+(2y)^2-4(2x)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x^2+y^2-2x=0;\quad\text{intended (d)}}.(2x)2+(2y)2−4(2x)=0⟹x2+y2−2x=0;intended (d)​.

It is a circle with centre (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) and radius 1. Exclude (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) from the exact locus of nonzero chords: it would give B=OB=OB=O, so the endpoints would not be different.

Reverse check: for any other point on the derived circle, B=(2x,2y)B=(2x,2y)B=(2x,2y) is a distinct original boundary point. The segment OBOBOB has midpoint MMM, so every retained locus point is attainable.

Another geometric view: original centre C=(2,0)C=(2,0)C=(2,0) gives CM⊥OMCM\perp OMCM⊥OM whenever M≠CM\ne CM=C. Thus (x−2,y)⋅(x,y)=0(x-2,y)\cdot(x,y)=0(x−2,y)⋅(x,y)=0, the same equation. The exceptional case M=CM=CM=C is valid too: it is the midpoint of the diameter joining (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) and (4,0)(4,0)(4,0).

Question 11 — A pole is the point associated with a polar line

PDF page 87 | MCQ | Notes: C12

The pole of the line 3x+4y=83x+4y=83x+4y=8 with respect to the circle x2+y2=16x^2+y^2=16x2+y2=16 is

First recall what a pole means. For x2+y2=r2x^2+y^2=r^2x2+y2=r2, the point P=(x1,y1)P=(x_1,y_1)P=(x1​,y1​) is associated with the polar line xx1+yy1=r2xx_1+yy_1=r^2xx1​+yy1​=r2. When PPP is outside, that line joins its two tangent contacts.

3x+4y=8⟺6x+8y=16.3x+4y=8 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 6x+8y=16.3x+4y=8⟺6x+8y=16.

Comparing with xx1+yy1=16xx_1+yy_1=16xx1​+yy1​=16 gives

P=(6,8);(a).\boxed{P=(6,8);\quad\text{(a)}}.P=(6,8);(a)​.

Another view: the pole lies along normal (3,4)(3,4)(3,4), so write P=λ(3,4)P=\lambda(3,4)P=λ(3,4). Its polar is λ(3x+4y)=16\lambda(3x+4y)=16λ(3x+4y)=16. On the given line the bracket is 8, hence λ=2\lambda=2λ=2 and P=(6,8)P=(6,8)P=(6,8). Comparing coefficients directly is the shorter calculation.

Question 12 — A zero squared radius gives one point

PDF page 87 | MCQ | Notes: C01

Statement I: The equation x2+y2−2x−4y+5=0x^2+y^2-2x-4y+5=0x2+y2−2x−4y+5=0 represents a point circle.

Statement II: The equation x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0 always represents a real circle of radius g2+f2−c\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}g2+f2−c​.

Choose the correct option.

  • (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  • (b) Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  • (c) Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  • (d) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Complete squares instead of guessing from the general shape.

x2+y2−2x−4y+5=(x−1)2+(y−2)2.x^2+y^2-2x-4y+5 =(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2.x2+y2−2x−4y+5=(x−1)2+(y−2)2.

Both squares can add to zero only when x=1,y=2x=1,y=2x=1,y=2. So Statement I is true: this is a point circle.

Statement II says always. But the squared radius g2+f2−cg^2+f^2-cg2+f2−c may be positive, zero or negative. For example, x2+y2+1=0x^2+y^2+1=0x2+y2+1=0 has no real points. Thus Statement II is false.

I true, II false;(d).\boxed{\text{I true, II false;\quad (d)}}.I true, II false;(d)​.

Check the distinction: a formula containing a square root does not guarantee its input is nonnegative. Determine the real existence condition before naming a radius.

Expanding cancels both squares, leaving 6h+6k=186h+6k=186h+6k=18, or h+k=3h+k=3h+k=3. The given centre line says h=2kh=2kh=2k. Thus 3k=33k=33k=3, so C=(2,1)C=(2,1)C=(2,1).

Using the boundary point (0,0)(0,0)(0,0),

r2=22+12=5.\boxed{r^2=2^2+1^2=5}.r2=22+12=5​.

Check: its squared distance to (3,3)(3,3)(3,3) is (2−3)2+(1−3)2=1+4=5(2-3)^2+(1-3)^2=1+4=5(2−3)2+(1−3)2=1+4=5.

Another possible approach: the segment from (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) to (3,3)(3,3)(3,3) has midpoint (3/2,3/2)(3/2,3/2)(3/2,3/2) and slope 1. Its perpendicular bisector is y−3/2=−(x−3/2)y-3/2=-(x-3/2)y−3/2=−(x−3/2), or x+y=3x+y=3x+y=3. Intersecting it with x=2yx=2yx=2y gives the same centre. The squared-distance subtraction explains that bisector algebraically.

Question 27 — Parallel tangents keep the same normal

PDF page 88 | MCQ | Notes: C04

A tangent to x2+y2=9x^2+y^2=9x2+y2=9 which is parallel to the line 2x−y+5=02x-y+5=02x−y+5=0 is

Parallel lines keep the same normal. Any candidate parallel to 2x−y+5=02x-y+5=02x−y+5=0 has the form 2x−y+c=02x-y+c=02x−y+c=0.

For the radius-3 circle centred at the origin,

∣c∣22+(−1)2=3⟹c=±35.\frac{|c|}{\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}}=3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\pm3\sqrt5.22+(−1)2​∣c∣​=3⟹c=±35​.

The listed line with the correct direction and distance is

2x−y+35=0;(a).\boxed{2x-y+3\sqrt5=0;\quad\text{(a)}}.2x−y+35​=0;(a)​.

Check the options: (b) has centre distance 9/5≠39/\sqrt5\ne39/5​=3; (c) has distance 3/5≠33/\sqrt5\ne33/5​=3. Option (d) is tangent to the circle but has a different normal (1,−2)(1,-2)(1,−2), so it is not parallel to the given line.

The question asks for a tangent; the valid partner 2x−y−35=02x-y-3\sqrt5=02x−y−35​=0 need not appear among the options.

Question 28 — The farthest point is on the opposite end of a radius

PDF page 88 | Numerical value | Notes: C14

PC=32+42=5.PC=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5.PC=32+42​=5.

PQ≤PC+CQ=5+2=7.PQ\le PC+CQ=5+2=7.PQ≤PC+CQ=5+2=7.

PQ2=25+4−2(3x+4y)=29−2(3x+4y).PQ^2=25+4-2(3x+4y)=29-2(3x+4y).PQ2=25+4−2(3x+4y)=29−2(3x+4y).

Equality at the negative end occurs at the same Q=(−6/5,−8/5)Q=(-6/5,-8/5)Q=(−6/5,−8/5). This connects a geometric extreme to a dot-product bound and shows why the opposite radius direction is optimal.

Question 29 — A right central angle makes a square with the tangents

PDF page 89 | MCQ | Notes: C06

Thus the fourth angle at the tangent intersection PPP is 90∘90^\circ90∘. With equal adjacent radii OA=OB=3OA=OB=3OA=OB=3, OAPBOAPBOAPB is a square of side 3. Its diagonal is

OP=32.OP=3\sqrt2.OP=32​.

Rotating this configuration around the origin lets PPP trace the full circle

x2+y2=18;(c).\boxed{x^2+y^2=18;\quad\text{(c)}}.x2+y2=18;(c)​.

Question 30 — Equal fixed radii make equal centre distances

PDF page 89 | MCQ | Notes: C07,C14

A variable circle touches externally both the circles x2+y2=1x^2+y^2=1x2+y2=1 and x2+y2−6x+8=0x^2+y^2-6x+8=0x2+y2−6x+8=0. The locus of its centre is

  • (a) 2x−3=02x-3=02x−3=0
  • (b) x2+y2=4x^2+y^2=4x2+y2=4
  • (c) x−3=0x-3=0x−3=0
  • (d) 2y−3=02y-3=02y−3=0

Find the fixed centres and radii first. The first circle has centre C1=(0,0)C_1=(0,0)C1​=(0,0), radius 1. The second is

(x−3)2+y2=1,(x-3)^2+y^2=1,(x−3)2+y2=1,

so C2=(3,0)C_2=(3,0)C2​=(3,0) and its radius is also 1.

Let the variable circle have centre P=(x,y)P=(x,y)P=(x,y) and positive radius ρ\rhoρ. External tangency gives

PC1=ρ+1,PC2=ρ+1.PC_1=\rho+1,\qquad PC_2=\rho+1.PC1​=ρ+1,PC2​=ρ+1.

Thus PC1=PC2PC_1=PC_2PC1​=PC2​. Squaring and subtracting,

x2+y2=(x−3)2+y2⟹2x−3=0;(a).x^2+y^2=(x-3)^2+y^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{2x-3=0;\quad\text{(a)}}.x2+y2=(x−3)2+y2⟹2x−3=0;(a)​.

Does every point on that line work? At P=(3/2,y)P=(3/2,y)P=(3/2,y) the shared distance is 9/4+y2≥3/2\sqrt{9/4+y^2}\ge3/29/4+y2​≥3/2. Choose

ρ=9/4+y2−1≥12>0.\rho=\sqrt{9/4+y^2}-1\ge\frac12>0.ρ=9/4+y2​−1≥21​>0.

Then both original external-tangency conditions hold. So the entire perpendicular bisector is valid; there is no hidden missing interval.

Pattern: equal fixed radii let the unknown variable radius cancel. With unequal fixed radii, you would instead obtain a fixed difference of centre distances, a different locus.

Question 31 — An axis intercept is a chord, not a radius

PDF page 89 | Numerical value | Notes: C04,C13

An intercept is the full chord cut by the axis. On the yyy-axis, x=0x=0x=0, so the original circle becomes

y2+4y−12=0⟹(y+6)(y−2)=0.y^2+4y-12=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (y+6)(y-2)=0.y2+4y−12=0⟹(y+6)(y−2)=0.

Its endpoints are (0,2),(0,−6)(0,2),(0,-6)(0,2),(0,−6); hence

length=∣2−(−6)∣=8.\boxed{\text{length}=|2-(-6)|=8}.length=∣2−(−6)∣=8​.

Another possible approach: complete squares to get centre (3,−2)(3,-2)(3,−2) and radius 5. The centre distance to the yyy-axis is 3, so chord length =225−9=8=2\sqrt{25-9}=8=225−9​=8.

Question 32 — Concentric circles share their centre

Question 33 — Tangency turns an unknown slope into a distance equation

  • (b) 000 and 43\dfrac4334​

We need tangent directions through one known point, the origin. First complete squares:

(x−4)2+(y−2)2=4.(x-4)^2+(y-2)^2=4.(x−4)2+(y−2)2=4.

Thus C=(4,2)C=(4,2)C=(4,2) and r=2r=2r=2. A nonvertical line through the origin is y=mxy=mxy=mx.

∣4m−2∣m2+1=2.\frac{|4m-2|}{\sqrt{m^2+1}}=2.m2+1​∣4m−2∣​=2.

16m2−16m+4=4m2+4⟹4m(3m−4)=0.16m^2-16m+4=4m^2+4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4m(3m-4)=0.16m2−16m+4=4m2+4⟹4m(3m−4)=0.

Question 34 — Use the completed-square picture to test each claim

PDF page 89 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C03,C13

For the circle x2+y2−2x−4y−4=0x^2+y^2-2x-4y-4=0x2+y2−2x−4y−4=0 consider:

(a) It passes through (4,2)(4,2)(4,2).

(b) It touches the yyy-axis.

(c) The point (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) lies inside it.

(d) Its intercept on the xxx-axis is 252\sqrt525​.

The correct statements are

  • (a) (a) and (b) only
  • (b) (a), (c) and (d) only
  • (c) (b), (c) and (d) only
  • (d) (a) and (d) only

Complete squares once, then reuse the picture for all four statements.

(x−1)2+(y−2)2=9.(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=9.(x−1)2+(y−2)2=9.

So the centre is C=(1,2)C=(1,2)C=(1,2), radius 3.

(a) True: (4,2)(4,2)(4,2) is 3 units horizontally from the centre, so it is on the circle.

(b) False: the centre's distance from the yyy-axis is 1, less than 3. The axis cuts the circle in two points; it does not merely touch.

(c) True: (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) is the centre, so its distance is 0, less than the positive radius.

(d) True: on the xxx-axis, x2−2x−4=0x^2-2x-4=0x2−2x−4=0, giving x=1±5x=1\pm\sqrt5x=1±5​. Their gap is 252\sqrt525​.

(a), (c), (d) only;(b).\boxed{\text{(a), (c), (d) only;\quad (b)}}.(a), (c), (d) only;(b)​.

Another check for (d): the centre is 2 units above the xxx-axis, so its chord length is 232−22=252\sqrt{3^2-2^2}=2\sqrt5232−22​=25​. This checks the root-gap calculation geometrically.

Question 35 — The radius to an axis touching point is perpendicular to that axis

PDF page 89 | MCQ | Notes: C13

A circle touches the xxx-axis at (3,0)(3,0)(3,0) and passes through (1,2)(1,2)(1,2). Its equation is

  • (a) x2+y2−6x−4y+9=0x^2+y^2-6x-4y+9=0x2+y2−6x−4y+9=0
  • (b) x2+y2−6x−4y+13=0x^2+y^2-6x-4y+13=0x2+y2−6x−4y+13=0
  • (c) x2+y2−6x+4y+9=0x^2+y^2-6x+4y+9=0x2+y2−6x+4y+9=0
  • (d) x2+y2−3x−2y+9=0x^2+y^2-3x-2y+9=0x2+y2−3x−2y+9=0

The radius to an axis touching point is perpendicular to the axis. Since the touching point is T=(3,0)T=(3,0)T=(3,0), the centre must lie on the vertical line x=3x=3x=3. Write it as C=(3,k)C=(3,k)C=(3,k).

Its radius is ∣k∣|k|∣k∣, so the circle equation is

(x−3)2+(y−k)2=k2.(x-3)^2+(y-k)^2=k^2.(x−3)2+(y−k)2=k2.

The supplied point (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) gives

(1−3)2+(2−k)2=k2⟹4+4−4k+k2=k2.(1-3)^2+(2-k)^2=k^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4+4-4k+k^2=k^2.(1−3)2+(2−k)2=k2⟹4+4−4k+k2=k2.

Hence k=2k=2k=2. We did not need to assume the centre was above the axis; the data proves it.

(x−3)2+(y−2)2=4⟹x2+y2−6x−4y+9=0;(a).(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x^2+y^2-6x-4y+9=0;\quad\text{(a)}}.(x−3)2+(y−2)2=4⟹x2+y2−6x−4y+9=0;(a)​.

Check both conditions: putting y=0y=0y=0 gives (x−3)2=0(x-3)^2=0(x−3)2=0, so there is exactly the one touching point (3,0)(3,0)(3,0). Substituting (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) gives 4+0=44+0=44+0=4 in the completed-square form.

After this chapter

Most routes begin with the same three steps: find the centre, find the squared radius and draw the needed radius or perpendicular. Use a direct geometric quantity when the question only asks for a length or count; find coordinates when they add information or provide a useful check. The original practice questions and their formats are preserved. Q10's nonzero-chord locus excludes the origin. All supporting methods and alternative views are visible for the later booklet.
